checks.label: An inverse function takes the output and does the opposite to get back to the input: on the first screen sin takes 30° to 0.5, the calculator keys sin⁻¹ of the drawn 150 ÷ 300 = 0.5 and gives back 30, the angle the triangle is drawn at, and sin⁻¹ undoes sin at every whole angle from 0° to 90°

When you bend an offset the conduit forms a right triangle, the offset depth the vertical (opposite) side and the distance between bends the diagonal (hypotenuse): the first screen marks 150 mm on the upright opposite side and 300 mm on the diagonal hypotenuse, drawn to one scale with a square corner

Sine is the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse, cosine the adjacent side to the hypotenuse, and tangent the opposite side to the adjacent side: on the keys screen sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ each light exactly that pair of sides, and every angle puzzle's answer is the inverse of that ratio of its drawn sides

Scientific calculators should be in degrees mode for trigonometry: every calculator drawn, on every screen and in every answer state, is marked DEG, and its inverse key gives degrees, sin⁻¹ 0.5 = 30 where radians would give 0.524

For 30 degrees sin(30) = 0.5, so the cosecant is 1/0.5 = 2.0; for 45 degrees sin(45) = 0.7071, so the cosecant is 1/0.7071 = 1.414: the calculators show 1 ÷ sin 30 = 2 and 1 ÷ sin 45 = 1.414, worked out as one over sin, beside sin⁻¹ 0.5 = 30, an angle

A 100 N force at 30 degrees has Fx = 100 N • cos 30° = 86.6 N and Fy = 100 N • sin 30° = 50.0 N: the arrow screen opens at 100 N and 30° with exactly these on its floor and wall shadows, each measured off the drawn arrow

To find the vertical component of a force the sine function can be used, and for the horizontal component the cosine: at every whole angle from 0° to 90° the wall shadow is the drawn arrow's height and reads F sin θ, the floor shadow its width and reads F cos θ, and turning the arrow up shortens the floor shadow and lengthens the wall shadow while the arrow keeps its length

Resolve forces in horizontal and vertical components restricted to the first quadrant: dragging the arrow's tip anywhere turns it no further than 0° or 90°, so neither shadow is ever negative, and run backwards each shadow stays between 5 N and 100 N

Run backwards, the shadows give the arrow back: for every pair of shadows, the arrow is drawn from the corner to the point they mark, with the handles on the shadows' ends, θ reads tan⁻¹(wall ÷ floor) and F reads √(floor² + wall²); switching from 100 N at 30° gives back 30.0° and 100.0 N

On the slope the weight W points straight down and its parts lie along the slope and square to it: at every whole tilt from 0° to 40° the part down the slope is W sin α and the part into it W cos α, both measured off the drawing, the weight is α away from the line square to the slope, and 500 N on 20° gives 171.0 N and 469.8 N

The line y = 0.5x is drawn with the same scale on both axes: the ticks on both axes are the same distance apart, the line climbs 0.5 for each 1 across, the triangle under it has rise ÷ run = 0.5 measured off the drawing, and its angle is tan⁻¹ 0.5 = 26.6°
Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, every wrong answer has its own hint and its own red row of working, and before an answer nothing in the picture shows the answer

No label sits on another label, a line or a handle, or runs off the picture, on any screen in any state: puzzles answered right, wrong or with Why? open, the arrow at every angle and run backwards at its smallest and largest shadows, the slope at every tilt
Every demonstration has finished within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; each answer, Why? and switch has settled within 1.8 s
